There's been a fount lately of anti-Southern sentiment everywhere and foolish distraction over an antiquated flag. For a change of pace, I thought I'd post this link -- HORACE KING: The Bridge Builder

I grew up in Alabama but didn't know of this man until about 15 years ago. I am baffled as to why Hollywood hasn't made a movie of the story of his life. This genius of a man pre-dates the civil rights era by more than 100 years.

Summary: Slave with no formal education, owned by a builder, demonstrates genius mechanical engineering abilities, builds most of the major covered bridges in the South and the stairway in the Alabama Capitol building. Makes himself and his master rich, buys his own freedom, partners with his former master (names his son after him, btw, an apparent gesture of friendship and respect), and this black man is elected to the Alabama House of Representatives in 1868!

Horace King was a genius and civil rights pioneer that few have ever heard of. Please, re-share this and spread the word.

Edit: He also looks a bit like Norm McDonald.﻿
The little-known engineering genius and civil rights pioneer, Horace King

It was a little disconcerting to learn:

In the 1850s in Columbus, Horace King purchased a slave named Sella. When King attempted to subdue Sella by flogging him, King was disappointed by the slave's resistance and quickly sold Sella to a slave trader.

I got to wondering how many freed slaves wound up as slaveholders themselves. Found an interesting article on the same from black news site The Root here. From the article:

A free black in Trimble County, Kentucky, " … sold his own son and daughter South, one for $1,000, the other for $1,200." … A Maryland father sold his slave children in order to purchase his wife. A Columbus, Georgia, black woman -- Dilsey Pope -- owned her husband. "He offended her in some way and she sold him … " Fanny Canady of Louisville, Kentucky, owned her husband Jim -- a drunken cobbler -- whom she threatened to "sell down the river." At New Bern, North Carolina, a free black wife and son purchased their slave husband-father. When the newly bought father criticized his son, the son sold him to a slave trader. The son boasted afterward that "the old man had gone to the corn fields about New Orleans where they might learn him some manners."

Day-um.

Wow. I've admired King for years but had no idea that he, himself, was a slave owner. That tempers my admiration a bit and, I think, will give me prompt to do a little more reading. Thanks for sharing that.

As for the rest, that's mind-boggling. One assumes that anyone freed from slavery themselves would somehow just inherently embody some kind of modern human-rights mindset. Not only was that not the case, the "slavery mindset" was so engrained and pervasive that it was apparently just a perfectly normal thing to do. I have to wonder if they reconciled it to themselves, even subconsciously, as sort of "degrees of being a bad owner" -- kind of like "It's ok for me to own you because I treat you better than you'd get treated somewhere else."

It's hard enough to explain modern politics to my kids and capture all of the relevant aspects of character and circumstance. In a similar vein, I was deeply moved and troubled by an excellent documentary, "The Rise and Fall of the Third Reich," which gave a tremendously personal and insightful treatment of how the Nazis rose to power from a populace of ordinary, decent people not unlike me or my neighbors. Point being, the passage of time is a massive distiller and simplifier and much that is needed to understand the American slavery era is forever lost. Apparently there was a lot about it that seemed "right" to a surprising number of people, slaves included. That is exactly what scares me about our times. Just what are we rationalizing and accepting today that will apall our grandchildren?
